question: In the lecture, it was shown that if a function \(f\) is differentiable on an open interval \((a,b)\) and attains a relative maximum at a point \(c\in(a,b)\), why must the derivative \(f'(c)\) equal zero? Use the definition of the derivative as a limit to justify your reasoning.

question: Consider the limit definition of the derivative \(f'(c)=\lim_{x\to c}\frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}\). Explain how the fact that \(c\) lies in the interior of an open interval \((a,b)\) guarantees that the limit can be approached from both sides, and why this is essential for concluding that \(f'(c)=0\) when \(f\) has a relative maximum at \(c\).
answer: Since \(c\in(a,b)\), there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \((c-\delta,c+\delta)\subset(a,b)\). Thus \(x\) can approach \(c\) from both the left and the right while remaining in the domain, allowing us to evaluate the two one‑sided limits of the difference quotient. These one‑sided limits yield the inequalities that force \(f'(c)=0\). If \(c\) were an endpoint, one side would be missing, and we could not conclude the derivative must be zero.

What role does the existence of a point \(c\) with \(f'(c)\ge 0\) play in this argument?

question: In the lecture it was shown that a constant function has derivative zero everywhere. Suppose a function \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and satisfies \(f(a)=f(b)=0\). Explain why, regardless of whether \(f\) is constant or not, there must exist at least one point \(c\in(a,b)\) where \(f'(c)=0\).
answer: Because \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that \(f\) attains a maximum and a minimum on \([a,b]\). If \(f\) is not constant, at least one of these extrema occurs at an interior point, and by Fermat’s theorem the derivative at that point must be zero. If \(f\) is constant, its derivative is zero everywhere, so the conclusion holds trivially. Thus in either case there exists \(c\in(a,b)\) with \(f'(c)=0\).

If we use a midpoint method to approximate the derivative of a constant function at any point, what value does the method produce, and why does this agree with the analytical derivative of a constant function?
answer: A midpoint method approximates the derivative by evaluating the function at the midpoint of an interval. question: Given a function \(f\) that is continuous on a closed interval \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), the Mean Value Theorem guarantees a point \(c\) where the tangent is parallel to the secant line. Discuss how the closed interval property ensures the existence of such a tangent, particularly addressing the role of the endpoints.

The Mean Value Theorem requires continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval to ensure that the secant line connecting \((a,f(a))\) and \((b,f(b))\) is well‑defined. The endpoints provide the two points that determine this secant slope \(\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\). Because \(f\) is continuous at \(a\) and \(b\), the values \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) exist and the secant slope is finite, allowing the theorem to assert the existence of a point \(c\in(a,b)\) where \(f'(c)\) equals that secant slope. Without continuity at the endpoints, the secant slope might not be defined, and the conclusion would fail.

question: Consider a differentiable function \(f\) on \([a,b]\) with \(f'(x)\ge 0\) for all \(x\in(a,b)\). By applying the mean value theorem, derive an inequality that bounds the difference \(f(b)-f(a)\) in terms of the maximum value of \(f'\) on \([a,b]\). answer: By the mean value theorem there exists \(c\in(a,b)\) such that \(f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a)\). Because \(f'(c)\ge 0\), we have \(f(b)-f(a)\ge 0\).
